title: Two die separately in RCMP custody
article: Two Yukoners died in RCMP custody over the weekend in separate incidents on the South Klondike Highway.

Heather Lynn Benson, 37, died early Saturday morning in a fatal rollover as she sat in the back of a Carcross detachment police cruiser en route to Whitehorse for a bail hearing scheduled for later in the day.
The Tagish woman died at the highway scene.
The next afternoon, 34-year-old Clark Edward Whitehouse died after an M-Division RCMP traffic officer who'd been investigating the Saturday crash pulled him over.
Whitehouse was arrested after fleeing from police and was in custody when he started to foam at the mouth. He was taken to Whitehorse General Hospital but pronounced dead on arrival.

Hours before the crash on Saturday morning, Benson had been arrested on drug charges after police executed a search warrant. She was then taken to the Carcross detachment, M-Division RCMP's Sgt. Pat Egan explained at a press briefing this morning in Whitehorse.
Const. Jeff Monkman then transported the woman in a police car into Whitehorse for court, usually set for 10 a.m. on weekends.
At about 5:45 a.m., Monkman's cruiser left the road approximately 20 to 25 kilometres south of the Carcross Cutoff and rolled.
Emergency Medical Services and a coroner were called to the scene and the coroner pronounced Benson dead.
"The RCMP regrets the circumstances that have led to this tragedy and wish to express its deepest sympathies to the Benson family," said Egan, who heads up the division's criminal operations.
The RCMP's traffic and major crimes units are investigating why the crash occurred.
"This isn't done in isolation," he said of the investigation. "This is done in conjunction with the coroner's office."

The constable was unhurt and has since been assigned to duties at RCMP headquarters in Whitehorse. The investigation must be completed before it's determined whether Motor Vehicles Act or criminal charges are warranted against the constable, Egan said.
Police cruisers have seatbelts in the back seats, but whether Benson was wearing one is part of the ongoing investigation, the sergeant said.

There are times prisoners don't wear seatbelts because it would be unsafe for an officer to put his arm or head into the back seat area, Egan said. It's up to the individual officer to make that call, he added.
He wouldn't say if Benson was wearing handcuffs at the time.

On Sunday afternoon, the traffic unit collision reconstructionist checking over the crash site on the South Klondike Highway had wrapped up his on-scene investigation and was headed back to Whitehorse when he saw Whitehouse's black pickup at about 1 p.m.
The lone driver was seen breaking the territory's Highway Traffic Act, Egan said.
When the officer used his lights and siren to get the pickup driver to pull over, the man didn't stop.
After a short vehicle chase, Whitehouse turned down Lewes Lake Road and fled on foot.

While the officer ran after Whitehouse, he could see the man ingesting a substance. Police believe it was cocaine, said Egan, noting more of the drug was found at the scene where Whitehouse was finally arrested.
The Whitehorse man refused to stop running and "exhibited combative behaviour", resulting in the officer taking out his M-26 Taser and using it to subdue Whitehouse and arrest him.
At that point, Whitehouse didn't exhibit any ill effects from the Taser's use, said Egan.

It wasn't until several minutes later when he'd walked back to the police cruiser and was sitting in the back seat that he started showing signs of medical distress, the sergeant said. White froth had started to develop at Whitehouse's mouth.
The policeman called for an ambulance and performed CPR until ambulance attendants arrived. Whitehouse was taken to hospital by Emergency Medical Services, where he was pronounced dead.
The RCMP's major crimes unit and the coroner's office are investigating.
There is no RCMP policy against using a Taser on a person under the influence of drugs.
"There has not been a documented case in North America where the Taser has caused a death," said the sergeant.

Often called a "stun gun," a Taser emits an electric shock that essentially jams the signals between a person's brain and muscles, causing the muscles to contract and the person to be immobilized. Once the trigger is released, the effects are gone.
The RCMP started looking into "less-lethal" ways to subdue violent individuals in the early '90s, leading to the addition of pepper spray and asp batons, which extend with the flick of the wrist.
The M-26 Taser uses 50,000 volts and 26 watts of electricity.
Yukon RCMP aren't naming the officer who arrested Whitehouse.
Autopsies will be conducted on both Benson and Whitehouse to determine the cause of death.
Coroner's inquests are routinely held in cases of in-custody deaths.
